title: Pravda Replikanta — Young Explorers Edition
lead: Why robots drop things and why they should check who is giving instructions.

news.title: How a robot hand learns not to drop things
news.summary: Researchers taught a LEAP hand to turn objects while holding them.
news.details: Training began in simulation, a computer model, and was then tested on a physical hand.
news.technical_novelty: An extra safety filter reduces the chance of dropping an object.
news.engineering_impact: The idea could help robots handle everyday items more carefully.
news.limitations: Across 13.3 hours, the team tested more than 4,800 unseen goals on four objects; the filter cut drops by 75%, but did not eliminate them.
news.evidence_status: Research experiments by the authors, not a test of every possible object.
news.body:
Try turning a pencil between your fingers without dropping it. A robot has to coordinate several fingers too. Researchers first trained a LEAP hand in simulation, a computer model, and then tested it on a real hand.

Over 13.3 hours, they tried more than 4,800 new goals with four objects. An extra safety filter reduced drops by 75%, but some still happened. That is why we should count mistakes, not just watch the best-looking demonstration.

news.title: Why a robot should check permission
news.summary: NTT Docomo developed a system that checks whether a robot may follow a command.
news.details: An A2A Gateway connects an AI assistant to a robot and checks rules before passing instructions along.
news.technical_novelty: The system also records actions and considers people nearby.
news.engineering_impact: Different people may have different rights to control robots in schools, hospitals or homes.
news.limitations: The company has not provided independent safety measurements from large-scale use.
news.evidence_status: Official company announcement, not proof of perfect autonomy.
news.body:
Imagine a robot at school that can open doors. Should it open every door for anyone who asks? No: it first needs to check permission. NTT Docomo developed a system that checks rules before sending a command to a robot.

It also records what the robot did and is designed to consider people nearby. That is a useful idea, but the announcement does not prove that the system never makes mistakes. Who should decide which instructions are allowed?

technology_signal.title: Being able to move is not the same as acting carefully
technology_signal.summary: Dexterous fingers and permission checks solve different safety problems.
technology_signal.implications: Good experiments count mistakes as well as successes.
